author: Akien (the observation and the question); CC's response appended and marked as a translation
acted_on_note: This observation drove Law 5's restatement (2026-08-17) + three tickets: history-reach-feeds-a-migration (BUILDME), a-dated-append-in-a-charter-is-a-red (PROVEME:waiting), an-artifact-is-present-tense-or-past-tense-never-both (PROVEME:waiting). The 'present-tense or past-tense, never both' principle is codified.
prose:
AKIEN (verbatim, 2026-08-15): So I have an observation that this would be a good time to discuss before we move on. the history creates noise. opus will see a thing as true because of an outdated bit of history... because even beyond me trying to keep history he does too. More information than I would. my first thought was: intention based programming means we NEVER do something part way. like a migration. because then we have multiple states in the system. now that doesn't mean we should never migrate something slowly, but it should be the exception not the rule. in the same vein, once history is done enough, maybe we move it out. or summarize it. have summarizing passes periodically? i dunno. so I'm asking: how should we handle this?

CC'S RESPONSE IN THE SAME DISCUSSION (a translation, marked as one; he pointed at 'the above' meaning both): The mechanism is tense — the Laws are present-tense contracts, history is past-tense record, and a model reader weights whatever is in context as if it were present tense. The biggest leak is that we write history INTO the present-tense artifacts: charters accreting dated paragraphs ('THE SECOND REGISTRATION SURFACE (ticket ..., 2026-08-15)', 'PARTIALLY RETIRED 2026-08-15'), CLAUDE.md carrying dated rulings inline, code comments carrying headstones. The proposed rule, taken as one: every artifact is either present-tense or past-tense, and nothing is both. Present-tense artifacts (charters, CLAUDE.md, state) get REWRITTEN at each design shift so they read as if written fresh today, provenance shrunk to a pointer (a ticket id), never a narrative — git already keeps every old version, so rewriting loses nothing. Past-tense artifacts (history, slates, voyages) stay append-only per Law 7, untouched, but are never loaded by default — opening one is deliberate archaeology. On migrations: atomic-in-one-voyage as the default (the rung move, b501bd5, is the precedent); a slow migration is legitimate exactly when it is a cast ticket whose cursor is the ONE statement of how far along — the defect is not partway-ness, it is partway with no single owner of the fact; two spellings coexisting with no ticket is the thing to forbid. On summarizing passes: no periodic pass (a poll); the event already fires — the PROVED crossing's charter delta IS the summarizing pass; sharpen it so the charter write rewrites to present tense and the voyage narrative freezes into history in the same act. Enforcement eventually (Law 4): a shape-check that reds dated-append patterns (RETIRED, formerly, date-stamped paragraphs) inside intention+why.json, and a briefing surface (charter + state, never history) that structurally excludes history. The generalization, covering CC's own memory too: any store a mind loads by default must hold current truth only; append-only stores exist but are opened, not loaded. This is Law 9 turned on the corpus's prose: an older paragraph is not evidence about the current design.
